sentences.text: The first time happened in the July she was eleven and it lasted about four seconds.
She was lying on the bank on her front, about three metres from the reeds, watching it.
It had been there for perhaps a minute doing the thing they do, which is nothing whatsoever with the body while the head goes round.
Then it took off, and came back, and landed in the same place.
It is worth saying what that looks like at three metres, because most people have only seen dragonflies going past.
It does not flutter and it does not settle.

It goes from stationary to about eight metres away in something under a second, in a straight line, and then it is stationary again in mid-air over the water — properly stationary, not hovering with effort — and then it is back on the reed, and the whole excursion has taken perhaps three seconds and there has been no part of it in which the animal looked like it was making an effort.
And the pond changed.
Not dramatically and not all at once and not, at first, in any way she could name.
Something about the light.
Something about the noise, which went slightly down.
Then she saw the willow.
The willow was standing up.
It came down in the January of 2015 in a gale and Elin had been in the kitchen when it went and had heard it, and she had walked past its trunk lying in the water every summer of her conscious life.
And there it was, upright, on the far bank, in leaf, a different shape entirely.
She looked at the rest of it and the jetty had planks on it.
And there was a boy on the far bank.
He was sitting on the end of the jetty with his feet not in the water and he was doing nothing.
He had his elbows on his knees.
He was perhaps eleven or twelve and he was wearing a red T-shirt and he was looking at the reeds at the north end, which is to say approximately at her, and he did not react in any way at all.
Then the dragonfly moved, and the willow was lying down, and the jetty was four posts, and the bank was empty.
Nothing came with it.
No sound, no cold, no smell, none of the things people ask about.
The transition in both directions was instantaneous and she did not feel it happen either time; there was a pond, and then there was a different pond, and then there was the pond.
Elin lay on the grass for a considerable time.
She was eleven.

What she did about it, over the following week, was to construct four explanations, of which the strongest was that she had fallen asleep in the sun, and she was reasonably satisfied with that until it happened again at thirteen while she was standing up.
